checkpoints: Line coverage only proves a line ran at least once under some test — it says nothing about which input cases ran or what was actually verified.

The classic failure case: a single happy-path test with a mocked dependency returning one row of data runs every line and reads as high coverage, yet never exercises the empty-array, negative-quantity, or not-found branches, and its assertion validates almost nothing.
That is exactly why 100% coverage can still coexist with a fragile, low-value test suite.

Mutation testing is the real signal: it deliberately changes the code (flips a comparison, deletes a branch) and checks whether any test catches it, measuring whether tests actually catch a regression rather than merely whether lines execute.
The practical policy is to treat coverage as a floor — investigate when it's low, but don't celebrate when it's high.
Enforce the coverage threshold per meaningful logic file rather than uniformly across wiring and configuration code.
Spend effort on edge-case branch coverage and assertion quality rather than chasing the coverage percentage itself.
A modern runner builds actionability checks into every action, so it synchronizes on real state instead of guessing at time — it never has to guess how long to wait.

Before it clicks or fills anything, it confirms the element is attached to the DOM, visible, enabled, stable (not mid-animation or mid-layout-shift), and able to receive events — only once ALL of those hold does the action fire.
A fixed sleep is exactly a guess, and guesses are wrong in both directions: too short on a slower CI box (flakes), dead time on a faster run (wasted).

Swapping sleeps for actionability checks removes roughly the classic 90% of sleep-based flakiness, because that flakiness was never really about timing — it was about acting on an element before it was truly ready.
The remaining minority doesn't come from the mechanism failing; it comes from a genuinely slow operation (a heavy render, a slow network call) that legitimately exceeds the wait's timeout.

The correct fix there is narrow — raise the timeout on that one locator or step, not add more sleeps or blanket-raise every timeout in the suite, which just re-introduces the same guessing problem at a bigger scale.

Time-based UI (a toast that appears after a delay, a debounced search box) is not a special case needing a sleep either — it's handled by an assertion with its own timeout that re-checks the condition on a tight polling loop until true, then proceeds immediately.
Every one of these rules collapses into a single principle: wait for a condition, never for a duration.

Commenting out the per-test cleanup hook while both flows share one test file turns Flow 2 into a hidden dependent of Flow 1: it asserts against the exact row Flow 1 just committed, so filtering to run Flow 2 alone, reordering the tests, or running them in parallel all break it immediately.
When an earlier flow in the same suite fails partway through, every flow that runs after it cascades into a false red even though nothing is actually wrong with that later flow's own logic.

A missing connection-pool teardown is a separate defect from the missing per-test cleanup, not a side effect of it — a suite can have full order independence restored and still leave the app/DataSource open at the end.

`app.close()` is what triggers `onModuleDestroy` and releases resources like the TypeORM connection pool; without it the Postgres socket stays open and the test runner cannot exit the process on its own.

Locally an unclosed handle shows up as a Ctrl+C annoyance, but in CI there is no one to kill the process, so the job runner waits for a natural exit and hangs until it burns its own timeout budget — real pipeline time lost on every run.

`expect(res.body).toEqual({...})` performs a strict deep comparison over the entire response body, so any field the server adds later breaks every test using it even when the core behavior under test is still correct.

Copying the actual received value of a nondeterministic field like `createdAt` into the expected object just to make a `toEqual` assertion pass is a sign the assertion is checking the wrong thing — a shape check such as `expect.any(String)` alongside a narrower `toMatchObject` on the fields that matter targets the real behavior instead.

Preserving the original speed win doesn't require deleting the cleanup outright — narrowing the truncate to only the table or rows the suite actually touches keeps most of the time savings while restoring test independence.

In an e2e suite, wall-clock time decomposes into N × boot cost + N × cleanup cost + N × actual request work; when the requests themselves take milliseconds, the fixture lifecycle (app boot, cleanup, re-seed) — not the tests' own logic — is what dominates the runtime.

A full app boot (compiling the Nest DI container and opening the TypeORM connection) produces a running app that is identical for every test in the file, so building it fresh inside `beforeEach` pays that cost N times for no benefit; moving it to `beforeAll` (or an equivalent once-per-file/shared-fixture scope) collapses N× boot cost to 1×, since what a test needs is a running app, not a newly compiled one.

A per-test `TRUNCATE ... CASCADE` that wipes every table — including reference/master data the tests never mutate — forces that reference data to be re-seeded before every single test even though it never changes; narrowing the truncate to only the tables the tests actually write to removes this redundant re-seed cost.

`RESTART IDENTITY` on a truncate keeps auto-increment IDs from leaking across tests even when the truncate scope is narrowed to just the mutated tables, so shrinking cleanup scope does not require giving up ID predictability between tests.

Reference/master data can be seeded once in `beforeAll` right after the app boots, with the single full-table wipe (including that reference data) deferred to `afterAll` right before the app closes — this replaces N re-seeds with one.

Narrowing what gets rebuilt or truncated per test does not change the isolation guarantee: every test still starts from an empty state for the tables it touches — only the mechanism producing that state gets cheaper, not what is promised to the test author.

Skipping the truncate of tables that tests actually mutate in order to save time is a different kind of change from narrowing cleanup scope: it lets mutated rows leak between tests and trades correctness for speed, which is why it must be rejected even under time pressure.

A speed-up claim needs two kinds of proof: running the suite with shuffled order or single-test (`.only`) isolation confirms no test silently depends on state left behind by another, and a recorded before/after wall-clock measurement confirms the suite actually got faster rather than the improvement being assumed.

A UI e2e suite that repeats a full browser login before every test pays that ~3s cost once per test for zero new information, since login success is already proven after the first test — the resulting suite slowdown scales with the number of tests, not with the number of distinct things being verified.

Recording a trace, video, and screenshot on every run regardless of outcome is a separate, unrelated cost from the login overhead: this data exists to aid debugging, but a passing test is never debugged, so paying the recording cost on passing runs buys nothing.

Playwright's `storageState` mechanism amortizes login across a suite: a `globalSetup` script performs the one real login the suite needs in its own browser context and serializes cookies and localStorage to a file; every other test's context then loads that file via `use.storageState`, starting already authenticated in a few hundred milliseconds instead of repeating the ~3s login flow.

The storage state file must be written only after the post-login redirect is confirmed (e.g., after `page.waitForURL` resolves), not the instant the login click resolves — saving state before the redirect lands bakes a half-authenticated or still-on-login-page session into the file, and every test that loads it then fails for a reason unrelated to what it actually tests.

The spec that verifies the login flow itself must still open a fresh browser context with no `storageState` loaded; reusing the shared authenticated state there would mean the login form is never actually exercised again, silently losing coverage on the exact mechanism the rest of the suite now depends on.

Amortizing login into one stored session introduces a new failure mode: the token baked into the storage state carries its own TTL, and if that TTL is shorter than the total suite runtime, tests running late fail with unrelated 401s that look like flakiness — mitigated by using long-lived tokens in the test environment or re-minting the storage state partway through a long run.

Playwright's `trace`, `video`, and `screenshot` options can be scoped to failure conditions instead of left always-on: `trace: 'on-first-retry'` and `screenshot: 'only-on-failure'` still capture everything needed to diagnose a failing test while adding zero recording cost to tests that pass.

The login-overhead fix and the diagnostics-overhead fix are independent because they have different root causes — redundant repeated work versus unconditional instrumentation — and different solutions — state caching versus conditional recording — so treating them as one problem risks fixing only half the slowdown.

The sketch centers on a single handlers module (an array mapping routes to responses over fixed demo data) with two thin bindings consuming it: one for the Node component-test runtime, one browser-side (service worker or the automation tool's route interception) for e2e; the lifecycle brackets the whole suite, with interception enabled at suite start and fully torn down at suite end.
Because one handlers module feeds both sides, mock data is defined exactly once — the two test suites can never drift apart on fixtures over time.
Fixtures must be frozen (fixed ids, fixed timestamps) because assertions — especially visual snapshots — are only repeatable over data that never moves.

Each test may push a scoped override that takes priority over the default; override-then-reset beats editing the default directly because an automatic hook after each test pops the override and restores the pristine default — scope is enforced by the test lifecycle itself, not by the test author's discipline, and mutating defaults directly lets an error-UI state leak into the next test.
Interception is enabled with the unmatched-request policy defaulting to ERROR, which turns a newly added fetch call from a silent 404/confusing UI state into an immediate, clearly named failure.

The honest boundary: this layer is a frozen snapshot of the API contract at the moment the handler was written — when the real backend changes its response shape, everything here stays green regardless.
Contract drift is deliberately delegated to a separate, thin test layer that runs against the real backend, outside this design's boundary, rather than pretending the mock layer already covers it.
The pipeline is capture → compare → (fail ⇒ artifacts for review) → human-approved baseline update, with provenance deciding everything else so it comes first.

Baselines are generated on the controlled CI image only, never a dev laptop, because macOS vs Linux CI render fonts/antialiasing/GPU differently — a laptop-minted baseline diffs against CI every run and the team learns to ignore red.
Baselines live in git so the PR that changes the UI carries the expected/actual/diff images as a first-class review artifact, not a surprise a customer reports later.

Comparison runs on a small pixel-ratio tolerance (~1%) — wide enough to absorb antialiasing jitter, tight enough that a 2px padding shift still fails as designed; 0% drowns PRs in false-positive noise, and a loose tolerance sleeps through real regressions.

Capture kills flakiness at the source: wait for fonts to be ready before the screenshot (the single best anti-flake step), disable animations so no transition is caught mid-frame, and stub dynamic content (timestamps, random IDs, ad slots) with fixed fixtures and pinned dates.
Masking a region is the fallback, used knowingly, never the first move — a real bug that lands inside a masked region becomes invisible, so mask only what truly cannot be stubbed.
Baselines are scoped per viewport/device project — mobile and desktop each keep their own baseline; sharing one baseline across sizes compares different renders and produces noise that means nothing.

An intentional redesign runs the baseline-regeneration job on CI and the resulting diff is approved by a reviewer inside the PR, exactly like any other code change — an auto-update-on-failure policy would systematically approve regressions along with real redesigns.

The failure signature (green every weekday, red exactly on Saturday) means the test depends on the ambient current system time without ever declaring that dependency — it isn't repeatable: the exact same code produces two different results at two different moments, violating the Repeatable criterion of F.I.R.S.T.
Fix family 1 controls the clock from the test side: pin the system time to a fixed instant so the weekend logic always sees exactly the chosen date, no longer dependent on the real CI run day.
Fix family 1 also fast-forwards the clock programmatically so an 'one hour later' behavior finishes in microseconds instead of requiring a real hour of wall time.

The mandatory companion rule is restoring the real clock after each test and scoping the fake clock to only the group that needs it, because a fake clock that leaks outside its scope breaks unrelated tests that have nothing to do with time.

Fix family 2 designs time out of the code entirely: make the functions pure, accepting a timestamp as a parameter instead of reading the system clock, so a test only needs to pass a fixed timestamp literal to be deterministic, with no faking mechanism required.

Only when a service genuinely must read 'now' internally (e.g., to log something or trigger a side effect) do you need to inject a clock (Clock in Java, TimeProvider in .NET, a clock function field in Go) and hand the test a fixed one in place of the real one used in production.
Runtime clock faking is the fastest shortcut on toolchains that support it out of the box.
Parameter passing/injection is the more portable design and the idiomatic, near-mandatory answer on stacks with no global fake-timer facility.

Both incidents trace back to the same structural limit of unit tests: a unit test only verifies one unit of logic against a contract IT defines itself, with no mechanism forcing two sides to agree over the real HTTP wire.

Incident A: each service unit-tests its own date serialization and each is 'correct' in isolation — only a real request crossing the actual wire format between the two services exposes the disagreement.
Incident B is exactly the trap the lesson calls 'the most common trap': the global ValidationPipe registered in main.ts does NOT automatically apply to an app built by Test.createTestingModule.
If beforeAll forgets to call app.useGlobalPipes again, the unknown field is never stripped in the test, the suite stays green, but production rejects the identical payload with 400.

The HTTP e2e layer is the only evidence layer precisely because it drives the ENTIRE pipeline unmocked: routing/prefix, validation, guards, handler, persistence, response serialization, all in one breath.

Parity is not equal across stacks: @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) boots the real Spring context and runs the full filter chain, and WebApplicationFactory<Program> reuses Program.cs directly — both inherit parity almost for free.

NestJS's TestingModule, by contrast, only builds the module graph and does not automatically carry main.ts's global pipe or prefix; Go hand-assembles http.ServeMux + middleware inside app.New(...), so a route that forgets to wrap its middleware silently diverges between test and production.

The way to close the gap is to keep a test that asserts an unknown field is rejected (or any other behavior depending on global config) — if someone forgets to re-register a global, that test FAILS immediately instead of letting production discover it via a real 400.

The mocking line sits at the process boundary — database access, HTTP calls, and the system clock are slow, shared, and non-deterministic, so they get replaced with doubles to keep a unit test fast and repeatable.

Everything living inside the module under test stays real: mocking a same-module collaborator welds the test to today's internal call structure, so a pure refactor (same behavior, different structure) still breaks the suite and erodes trust in the test.

Over-mocking has a second, worse cost: once everything is stubbed, assertions degrade into "the code called what it currently calls" — the test just restates the implementation and still passes even when the behavior is wrong.
The mechanism that makes boundary mocking clean is the injection seam: the service declares its dependency through the constructor, and the test supplies a double at exactly that point.
That seam can be a container overriding the provider's token, or, in a stack without a container, an interface plus a small hand-written struct mock (Go-style).
This way the test drives the real production wiring path, with a fake swapped in only at the edge.
For a pure function, the right amount of mocking is zero: feed inputs in, assert outputs out.
